id: from Second Book of Odes: 6. What the Chairman Told Tom

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Poetry? It’s a hobby. I run model trains. Mr Shaw there breeds pigeons. It’s not work. You dont sweat. Nobody pays for it. You could advertise soap. Art, that’s opera; or repertory— The Desert Song. Nancy was in the chorus. But to ask for twelve pounds a week— married, aren’t you?— you’ve got a nerve. How could I look a bus conductor in the face if I paid you twelve pounds? Who says it’s poetry, anyhow? My ten year old can do it and rhyme. I get three thousand and expenses, a car, vouchers, but I’m an accountant. They do what I tell them, my company. What do you do? Nasty little words, nasty long words, it’s unhealthy. I want to wash when I meet a poet. They’re Reds, addicts, all delinquents. What you write is rot. Mr Hines says so, and he’s a schoolteacher, he ought to know. Go and find work.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Poetry, Shaw, You

outputs.L1:
Poetry? It’s a hobby. I run model trains; Mr Shaw there breeds pigeons. It isn’t work. You don’t sweat. Nobody pays you for it. You could advertise soap. Art—that’s opera, or repertory: *The Desert Song*. Nancy was in the chorus.

But to ask for twelve pounds a week—you’re married, aren’t you?—you’ve got a nerve. How could I look a bus conductor in the face if I paid you twelve pounds? And who says it’s poetry, anyhow? My ten-year-old can do it—and rhyme.

I get three thousand, plus expenses, a car, and vouchers—but I’m an accountant. My company does what I tell it. What do you do? Nasty little words, nasty long words—it’s unhealthy. I want to wash whenever I meet a poet. They’re Reds, addicts—all delinquents.

What you write is rot. Mr Hines says so, and he’s a schoolteacher; he ought to know. Go and find work.
outputs.L2:
Poetry is merely a pastime. I play with model railways, and Mr Shaw keeps pigeons; neither activity counts as employment. There’s no physical effort involved, and no one gives you money for doing it. Why not earn a living writing soap advertisements instead? Real art means opera or repertory theatre—*The Desert Song*, for example. Nancy sang in its chorus.

And yet you expect twelve pounds every week! You’re married too, if I’m not mistaken. What cheek. If I gave you that much, I’d be ashamed to face a bus conductor. Besides, who decided your writing was poetry? My ten-year-old can produce verses, complete with rhymes.

I receive three thousand, plus expenses, a car, and vouchers—but I’m an accountant. My company follows my instructions. What useful purpose do you serve? All you produce are unpleasant words, short and long alike. It can’t be healthy; whenever I encounter a poet, I feel the need to wash. Poets are communists, drug users, and delinquents, the lot of them. Your writing is rubbish. Mr Hines agrees, and since he teaches at a school, he should understand such things. Stop this nonsense and get a proper job.
outputs.L3:
The speaker dismisses poetry as little more than an unpaid hobby, refusing to recognize it as legitimate work. He argues that poets do not deserve a substantial wage because their writing appears to involve neither visible effort nor practical value. In contrast, he presents his own profession as an accountant as respectable, authoritative, and deserving of financial reward. His well-paid position becomes the standard by which he judges the usefulness of others’ labor.

This contempt extends to poetry itself. He portrays poetic language as unhealthy, worthless, and so easy to produce that even a child could do it. By denying the skill and discipline involved in writing, he reduces poetry to meaningless wordplay. He also relies on stereotypes, depicting poets as suspicious or dangerous outsiders who fail to contribute properly to society. Ultimately, his instruction that they should find “real” work reveals a narrow, materialistic view of value—one that measures worthwhile labor solely through income, authority, and visible practical results.
outputs.L4:
The text uses a dismissive employer’s monologue to satirize society’s attitude toward poetry and other forms of creative labor. Speaking from a position of economic authority, the employer assumes that conventional, profitable work is inherently respectable, while writing poetry is idle, useless, and undeserving of financial reward. He treats productivity as the only meaningful measure of value: labor matters only when it produces visible goods, supports established institutions, or generates income. Because poetry does not fit neatly into this economic framework, he refuses to recognize it as genuine work.

His criticism extends beyond poetry’s supposed impracticality. He also portrays the poet as irresponsible or even immoral, suggesting that creative activity represents a failure to accept ordinary social duties. In his view, respectable people work regular jobs, obey accepted standards, and contribute in ways that can be measured materially. The poet’s different priorities therefore appear threatening. By presenting these assumptions through the employer’s exaggerated and self-satisfied speech, the text exposes the narrowness of a society that confuses profitability with usefulness and conformity with virtue.

The monologue also reveals the employer’s hypocrisy. Although he claims to judge others according to objective principles such as discipline, morality, and hard work, his judgments are shaped by prejudice and self-interest. He uses his social position as evidence that his opinions must be correct, never seriously considering the possibility that poetry may require effort, skill, or intellectual discipline. At the same time, he benefits from a system that gives people like him the authority to decide which activities deserve wages and respect. His condemnation of the poet is therefore not merely a personal opinion; it is backed by economic power.

Status plays an important role in this process. Because the employer controls access to money and employment, he can impose his definition of legitimate labor on those beneath him. The poet may possess imagination, knowledge, and artistic ability, but these qualities carry little weight when they are judged by someone who recognizes only conventional forms of success. Cultural ignorance thus combines with economic authority: the employer does not understand poetry, yet his power allows that lack of understanding to shape another person’s material circumstances.

Ultimately, the satire challenges the belief that market value and human value are the same. Poetry may not produce immediate profit, but it can preserve experience, question social assumptions, create beauty, and give language to emotions or ideas that ordinary discourse cannot express. By making the employer’s contempt appear prejudiced and absurd, the text invites readers to reconsider who has the power to define useful work. It suggests that society’s hierarchy of labor is not natural or impartial; it is created by those with wealth and status, whose limited cultural understanding may cause them to dismiss valuable forms of human activity simply because those activities cannot easily be bought, sold, or measured.
outputs.L5:
Poetry has a way of turning ordinary moments into something unforgettable. George Bernard Shaw once suggested that we do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing. The same might be said of imagination. Poetry keeps it alive, inviting us to look at the world with curiosity, humor, and courage.

Shaw used words to challenge society, expose hypocrisy, and inspire thought. You, too, carry the power to shape ideas through language. A single honest sentence can comfort someone, question an injustice, or reveal a feeling that seemed impossible to express.

Poetry does not belong only to famous writers. It belongs to you whenever you notice beauty, listen closely, and give your experience a voice.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical dramatic monologue in the voice of a smug, middle-class accountant dismissing a poet who has asked to be paid twelve pounds a week.
counterfactuals.output:
Twelve pounds a week?

My dear fellow, do sit down—  
not there; that chair is for clients.

Twelve pounds! I admire the imagination.  
One expects imagination from a poet, of course,  
though preferably confined to the poetry.  
In accounts, we find it troublesome.

Now, I have examined your proposal—  
if “proposal” is not too commercial a word—  
and nowhere do you indicate what, precisely,  
the firm receives for its twelve pounds.  
You mention “beauty,” “truth,” and “the human spirit,”  
but none appears to be a negotiable asset.  
Truth, indeed, is often a liability.

You say your poems will outlive us.  
Possibly. But they will not outlive the quarter  
unless they show a return.

Consider my own position.  
I rise at seven, take the 7:42,  
carry sandwiches wrapped by my wife,  
and spend eight hours reconciling what men desire  
with what they can deduct.  
That, sir, is creation.  
Every balanced column is a sonnet  
with the sentiment removed.

And what do you do?  
You stroll beside canals at noon,  
discover anguish in a sparrow,  
then invoice civilisation.

Twelve pounds would pay the girl in Filing,  
who is punctual, agreeable,  
and does not require despair to operate.  
It would nearly cover Mr Wilkins’s golf subscription—  
essential, you understand, to maintaining contacts.  
But for six pages on mortality?  
Mortality is universal.  
There is no scarcity value.

No, no—don’t speak of posterity.  
Posterity has never settled an account.  
If, in a hundred years, schoolchildren are compelled  
to memorise your verses,  
you may apply again, in writing,  
enclosing proof.

Until then, I can authorise two pounds ten  
for stationery, provided you submit receipts,  
and perhaps luncheon on publication day,  
excluding wine.

You look offended.  
That is the artistic temperament, I suppose:  
always wanting the world to feel,  
when what the world requires  
is simply to add up.

Good morning.

And do close the door quietly—  
there are people working.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem in which a philistine businessman argues that poetry is merely a hobby, compares it to model trains and pigeon breeding, and tells the poet to find real work.
counterfactuals.output:
He taps the ash from his cigar into a saucer and says poetry is a hobby, like model trains in a basement, little black engines circling forever beneath the furnace pipes, passing towns where no one buys or sells. Or pigeon breeding, he says, feeding gray birds that rise, wheel, and return with nothing in their beaks. He smiles as if he has balanced the books of heaven.

Find real work, he tells the poet. Make something people can use: a door, a ledger, a profit. The world pays for weight, for steel, for hours stamped on a card. It does not pay for moonlight trembling in a glass.

Outside his office window, the city lifts its soot-colored wings. Trains cry from the yards. A flock turns above the warehouses, suddenly silver, then vanishes into evening. The businessman closes the blinds, pleased with the dark he has earned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a 1960s British company executive interviewing a married poet for a job. Give the executive a prejudiced, rambling speech attacking poetry, artists, Reds, and addicts.
counterfactuals.output:
“Now, look here, Mr. Bell, I’m going to be perfectly frank. You say you’re married—which at least suggests some acquaintance with responsibility—but then you put down ‘poet’ under occupation. Poet! In my experience, that means a fellow who rises at noon, borrows cigarettes, and expects civilisation to applaud because he’s discovered a rhyme for ‘despair.’

We’re a commercial concern, not a coffee cellar in Soho. We deal in invoices, consignments, and facts—solid things that don’t require a chap in a black polo-neck to explain what they ‘really mean.’ You let one artist into an office and before long he’s painted the filing cabinets purple, called the lavatory a happening, and demanded a grant.

And poetry’s the thin end of it. Today it’s sonnets; tomorrow it’s pamphlets. Then come the Reds, all beards and brotherhood, explaining that the company belongs to the workers—though none of them has ever arrived before ten or lifted anything heavier than a placard. They despise profit right up to the moment they want an advance.

Then there’s the other lot: pills, powders, jazz until dawn, staring at one’s hands as if they’ve just been nationalised. They call it expanding the mind. In business we prefer the mind to remain approximately the same size and to be at its desk by nine sharp.

Still, perhaps marriage has knocked some of the moonlight out of you. Can you type? No? Add columns? No? Use a telephone without turning the conversation into blank verse? Hm. Well, we may have an opening in complaints. You seem professionally acquainted with misery.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abrasive monologue about society’s contempt for poets, using colloquial British language, references to bus conductors, repertory theatre, schoolteachers, and a salary of three thousand pounds plus expenses.
counterfactuals.output:
Poets? This country can’t stand them. Oh, it’ll stick a bronze plaque on the wall once they’re safely dead, once there’s no danger of them asking awkward questions or borrowing half a crown. But a living poet? Somebody who looks at the great grey British pudding and says it tastes of dust? No, thank you. Get a proper job, mate.

We’ll listen to a bus conductor bawling, “Move down inside!” as if he’s delivering the Sermon on the Mount. We’ll applaud some repertory theatre hack coughing through *The Importance of Being Earnest* in a damp hall in Coventry. We’ll let schoolteachers batter every spark out of a child’s head with dates, definitions and red ink. But let a poet speak plainly about loneliness, rot, desire—anything that hasn’t been approved by the council—and everyone suddenly remembers an urgent appointment.

That’s the trick, isn’t it? Society doesn’t hate poetry because it’s useless. It hates poetry because it’s impertinent. Poetry notices the smell behind the curtains. It sees the smug little man with his salary of three thousand pounds plus expenses, polishing his respectability while his soul goes mouldy in the stationery cupboard. And he knows it sees him. That’s why he sneers.

So don’t tell me Britain loves its poets. Britain loves them embalmed, footnoted and shoved onto a school syllabus where no one can hear them scream. A live poet is a nuisance. A dead poet is culture.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a darkly comic stream-of-consciousness speech from an accountant who boasts about his income and authority while insisting that poets do nothing useful and should not be paid.
counterfactuals.output:
Look, I don’t dislike poets. Dislike implies a cost center, an allocation of emotional resources, and frankly they haven’t submitted the proper form. I simply maintain—and the figures maintain with me—that poets produce nothing billable. Clouds, grief, the moon reflected in a puddle: none of these can be depreciated. I checked.

Meanwhile, I earn—well, one shouldn’t boast, but if one’s salary has six figures, the sixth figure begins to feel neglected unless introduced. I have a corner office, technically two corners if you count the angle behind the filing cabinet, and a chair that adjusts in nine directions, one of which I believe is moral superiority. When I lean back, departments tremble. When I clear my throat, stationery budgets lose ten percent.

That is usefulness.

A poet leans back and calls it “autumn.”

And then they ask to be paid! Paid for what? For placing “bone” near “telephone” and looking exhausted? I have looked exhausted for twenty-seven years and never once invoiced it separately. I make numbers reconcile. I take two columns that hate each other and force them into a balanced relationship until death or audit do them part. There’s your romance. There’s your tragedy. Sometimes there’s even a negative sign.

Do poets understand authority? I sign things. Blue ink. Permanent. A small movement of my wrist and someone’s conference becomes an email. Someone’s ergonomic mouse becomes a standard mouse. Someone’s livelihood becomes “headcount optimization.” I don’t enjoy it, obviously. Enjoyment is not tax-deductible.

Last year I received a bonus larger than the arts council’s annual budget. They gave me a plaque. Heavy glass. Could kill a man, or at least a sonnet. The inscription said EXCELLENCE IN FISCAL STEWARDSHIP, which is corporate poetry, except it has measurable outcomes and comes with parking.

Poets say they reveal truth. Wonderful. Let them reveal why Travel and Entertainment is up eighteen percent. Let them rhyme “unauthorized minibar” with “final written warning.” Let them scan the meter on a procurement irregularity.

No, no salaries for poets. Give them exposure. They adore exposure. Moonlight, winter branches, the pale face of mortality—exposure everywhere. If they wanted money, they should have developed a practical skill, like converting human panic into quarterly forecasts.

Of course, late at night, after the cleaners leave, I sometimes find a poem photocopied beside the printer. Anonymous. Something about a man counting coins in a burning house.

Ridiculous.

The house is insured.

I checked.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
